rv.q: It’s a hope that more queer protagonists deserve, dulled by a play trading in stereotypes.
But this is a fast, fearless, bracing piece of work.

Searingly funny and incisively acted, the Second Stage Theater production shows that psychological terror can assume the most mundane form, and that the individuals with whom we share both DNA and personal memories still can be mysterious strangers.
Its humor and heart speak to the complexity of belonging to a family.
The Visitors does at least disabuse its overwhelmingly Western, undeniably progressive audience of the illusion of choice.

Director Jenna Worsham, who collaborated with the author a few years back on the well-received “At the Wedding,” has recruited fine actors who make the characters consistently engaging, even when their actions become frustrating or challenge credibility.
There’s not an ounce of trust to go around, and each sibling is running their own battle campaign.
The good play and worthy performances would benefit from another visual concept or a more accommodating theater.
There’s an honesty to Turner’s characterizations in The Visitors, and a genuine humor, that justify spending time with this fractured family.
Bryna Turner’s sibling dramedy has enough bite to keep the family squabbling entertaining, but fussy staging and a familiar formula mean these visitors don’t linger long after they leave.

cn.t: Critics are mostly warm on *The Visitors*, praising Turner's sharp, satirical take on family dysfunction and a strong ensemble cast. A few find it uneven, but its darkly comic dissection of sibling obligation largely lands.

vr.q: So well acted, so enjoyable. I thought it was very funny. Had a great time in the theater with these this wacko family.
